criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access; focuses entirely on internal corporate governance, accounting, tax liability, procurement, decision-making autonomy, and institutional financing of Finnish waterworks.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines three public utility governance and legal-ownership models in Finland (municipal unit under the Municipality Act, municipal-owned enterprise, and municipal-owned company under the Limited-liability Companies Act, alongside procurement and cost-recovery statutes). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — although utility ownership structure can qualify when directly governing service access, here the governance models are analysed solely as internal corporate/financial management structures (bookkeeping separation, tax treatment, procurement compliance, board autonomy, and institutional investor access) rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from semi-structured interviews with 9 managers across 11 Finnish waterworks (plus FIWA and local authority representatives) and an online questionnaire of FIWA member waterworks managers (38 of 278 responding, 13.7% response rate), analysed via SWOT frameworks.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no outcome relevant to household or community service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Evaluated outcomes are internal organizational and financial attributes: business orientation, bookkeeping accuracy, financial/operational transparency, tax liability, municipal political interference in board decisions, and opportunities for institutional investors.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis (Finnish water and sewage utilities), exposure (MU, MOE, and MOC public governance models), qualitative managerial/financial outcomes, and descriptive qualitative interview/survey SWOT design are clearly identifiable, though the outcomes fall outside review scope.

evidence_quotes.quote: According to this study, restructuring appears to increase business orientation, improve accuracy in bookkeeping and, in some cases, increase transparency. The selection of the right governance model also provides opportunities for institutional investors.
The objective of this research is to study the three most common public governance models used in the Finnish water sector and evaluate how they affect the performance of waterworks.

The main source of empirical data were semi-structured interviews. The interviewees were selected among Finnish waterworks’ managers to represent the current state of the waterworks, different governance models and the water sector as well as possible.

According to the results of this research, restructuring waterworks from MUs into MOEs and MOCs appears to increase business orientation, improve accuracy in bookkeeping and, in the case of MOEs, increase transparency.

raw_response.exposure: Three Finnish public utility ownership and governance models: municipal unit (MU), municipal-owned enterprise (MOE), and municipal-owned company (MOC)
raw_response.outcome: Internal organizational and financial management attributes of waterworks (business orientation, bookkeeping accuracy, transparency of financial/operational information, tax treatment, political interference in board decision-making, and institutional investor financing opportunities)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Finnish public water and sewage utilities (semi-structured interviews with 9 managers in 11 waterworks plus representatives of FIWA and Finnish Local and Regional Authorities; online questionnaire with 38 responses from 278 FIWA member waterworks managers)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). While this qualitative empirical study examines public utility ownership and governance models in the Finnish water and sewage sector (MU, MOE, and MOC), it evaluates only internal corporate, accounting, and financial management attributes—specifically bookkeeping separation and accuracy, public disclosure/transparency, corporate tax treatment, municipal political influence over board decisions, business orientation, and opportunities for institutional investors. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no) and reports no outcome relevant to service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Accordingly, the paper is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive qualitative study using semi-structured interviews, an online manager questionnaire, and SWOT analysis
